node.label: Mrinalini Sinha
node.date_label: Colonial Masculinity (1995) · “Giving Masculinity a History” (1999) · Specters of Mother India (2006) · Political Imaginaries, co-edited (2022)
node.description: In Colonial Masculinity (1995), Sinha argues that the “manly Englishman” and the “effeminate Bengali” were changing political constructions through which colonial authority and nationalist resistance were negotiated. Her imperial social formation framework studies British and Indian politics together, making masculinity part of the explanation of imperial power. Specters of Mother India (2006) follows an international controversy to show how women’s collective activism briefly opened a different route to citizenship, before subsequent political settlements curtailed it. Antoinette Burton subsequently identified its framework as an important feminist model for connecting domestic and imperial histories. Specters received the Albion Book Prize and the Joan Kelly Memorial Prize in 2007. Sinha also questions an emphasis on fragmentary histories alone in Chakrabarty’s project, proposing intersecting global histories of rights and citizenship.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Colonial Masculinity: The “Manly Englishman” and the “Effeminate Bengali” in the Late Nineteenth Century (1995); “Giving Masculinity a History” (1999); Specters of Mother India: The Global Restructuring of an Empire (2006); Political Imaginaries in Twentieth-Century India (2022), co-edited with Manu Goswami.
node.scope_note: Read Specters introduction pp. 1–20 of 22 in a licensed preview; chapters, epilogue and endnotes unread. Colonial Masculinity is characterized through Hall’s signed review, Burton’s explicit reading and institutional bibliographic records; the book itself is unread. Giving Masculinity a History is abstract-only. Political Imaginaries is checked through frontmatter and contents only. Scott’s and Chakrabarty’s original works are not freshly read. Sinha’s foreword to Burton is read separately from Burton’s introduction.

proposed_edges.relationship: Sinha and Hall co-edit Cambridge’s Critical Perspectives on Empire series from 2006, a collaboration corroborated in the frontmatter of Scandal of Colonial Rule (2012).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sinha CV p. 1, Editorial Positions, names Hall and Wilson and dates this co-editorship from 2006; authorized 2012 frontmatter, PDF p. 2, lists all three as Editors. No individual book coauthorship or uninterrupted collaboration beyond the dated witnesses is inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: Sinha and Wilson co-edit Cambridge’s Critical Perspectives on Empire series from 2006, a collaboration corroborated in the frontmatter of Scandal of Colonial Rule (2012).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sinha CV p. 1, Editorial Positions; authorized 2012 frontmatter, PDF p. 2, lists Hall, Sinha and Wilson as Editors. Hall’s shared credit is retained. This supports editorial collaboration, not a common argument or coauthorship of Epstein’s book.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Imperial Optics” (2011), Burton identifies Colonial Masculinity (1995) and Sinha’s imperial social formation as a feminist model supporting her challenge to separate domestic and imperial histories.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Burton’s own introduction, printed pp. 10–11, especially p. 11 paragraph beginning “In spite of these limitations,” explicitly describes Sinha’s model as “crucial.” Re-read in licensed preview, physical PDF pp. 33–34. Credit to Stoler and Cooper in the following sentences remains shared; neither exclusive derivation nor personal supervision is claimed. Sinha’s full 1995 book and Burton’s unseen endnotes remain unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: imperial social formation as a feminist model

proposed_edges.relationship: In Specters of Mother India (2006), Sinha distinguishes Indian feminism’s simultaneous disavowal and constitution of communities from the paradox of sexual difference in Scott’s account of French feminism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sinha, introduction pp. 11–12, passage spanning the page break that explicitly names Scott. This is Sinha’s comparison of different historical configurations, not a claim that Scott’s French account is wrong in its own setting. Scott’s original work and Sinha’s endnote 35 were not read; its exact bibliographic identification is not asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Specters of Mother India (2006), Sinha accepts Chakrabarty’s problem of indispensable yet inadequate European categories but argues that fragmentary histories alone risk conceding an exclusively European origin to universal rights.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sinha, introduction pp. 15–16, from the paragraph naming Chakrabarty through her alternative of intersecting global histories. Her objection concerns an emphasis on fragments “alone,” and she retains the problem that motivates provincializing Europe. This is a qualified methodological disagreement, not a wholesale rejection. Chakrabarty’s originals and Sinha’s endnotes 45–48 remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Colonial Masculinity (1995) treats gendered colonial identities as historically produced in British–Indian political struggles; “Giving Masculinity a History” (1999) examines what colonial Indian historiography contributes to histories of masculinity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Hall’s review pp. 378–379 identifies the relational, changing categories in the 1995 book. The 1999 publisher abstract explicitly frames the contribution to masculinity historiography and feminist concern with gendered power. Full book and full 1999 article unread; claim stays at the argument and abstract level.

proposed_edges.relationship: Specters of Mother India (2006) locates women’s collective political agency at the centre of a contingent reworking of citizenship during the Mayo controversy and its aftermath.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sinha, introduction pp. 9–14: especially pp. 10–11 on a possible citizen-subject and its subsequent neutralization. The reading preserves Sinha’s limits concerning privileged protagonists, communal distinctions and the temporary character of the opening; no universal emancipation claimed. Later chapters and epilogue unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Specters of Mother India (2006) develops an imperial social formation approach that combines intersecting histories, multiple scales and contingent events across Britain, India and the United States.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sinha, introduction pp. 16–19, especially pp. 16–17 on widening and deepening analysis and pp. 17–18 on imperial ordering, uneven connections and cultural/material mediation. This is an explicit methodological proposal for global history, not an inference from the international subject matter. Remaining introduction pp. 21–22, chapters and notes unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Specters of Mother India (2006), Sinha argues that postcolonial critiques of liberal rights have not attended sufficiently to the alternative trajectories of rights in women’s collective struggles.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sinha, introduction pp. 12–13, paragraph beginning “Postcolonial critiques” and its continuation. She recognizes those critiques’ achievements while identifying an opening for an alternative genealogy; this does not deny colonial exclusion or endorse every liberal universal. A field-level criticism distinct from the named fragmentary-history objection at pp. 15–16. Chapters and endnotes unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: questions limits of postcolonial rights critiques

proposed_edges.relationship: In the introduction to Manliness and Masculinities in Nineteenth-Century Britain (2005), John Tosh cites Sinha's 'Giving Masculinity a History' (1999) as the sole reference for his statement that historians now study masculinity in specific historical conjunctures alongside other identities and structuring principles.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the introduction’s discussion on printed p. 8 and its note 18 on printed p. 9 in the licensed publisher preview. The body argues for interpreting masculinity within specific conjunctures involving other identities and organizing principles; its directly attached note identifies Sinha’s 1999 essay alone, specifically p. 446. This is a citation supporting a substantive methodological claim in the body, rather than a collective reading recommendation. The proposal records that limited use of her argument; it does not assert a general intellectual debt or adoption of her entire imperial framework. The collection’s original year is 2005, also given by the publisher’s indexed first-edition listing and the preview copyright; the preview reproduces a 2016 Routledge issue. The preview’s inconsistent first-publication line is not used for dating. The original Sinha essay and Tosh’s later chapters were not read for this proposal.
